narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 94% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it is high enough that the admissions decision treated you as very unlikely to succeed without significant change.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in the second decile, below the roughly sixth-decile average among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the next most influential factor; at 28 it was well below the accepted-student average of about 37, again increasing the predicted risk. Your first-year class-rank decile was third in importance, and your second-decile standing there also pushed toward failure. In other words, the model focused most on your later law-school grades, then your admissions test score, then your early grades—all suggested academic preparation below the profile associated with passing.

To move forward, ask admissions for feedback, meet with an advisor, and build a concrete improvement plan. If possible, retake the LSAT after structured preparation, and consider coursework or a program that demonstrates stronger academic readiness. Address any circumstances that affected your grades, apply to schools with holistic review, and plan ahead for bar-exam support. A future application should show measurable improvement in the areas the model weighted most heavily.
